Finally, the algorithm is implemented on a simulator, and the reconstructed spectrum is verified against a classical computational reference. The low cost of our algorithm makes it attractive to use on fault-tolerant quantum devices to accelerate the development and commercialization of high-capacity battery cathodes.
item.dc:creator: Stepan Fomichev, Pablo A. M. Casares, Jay Soni, Utkarsh Azad, Alexander Kunitsa, Arne-Christian Voigt, Jonathan E. Mueller, Juan Miguel Arrazola

item.title: Trotterization, Operator Scrambling, and Entanglement
item.description: arXiv:2506.23345v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Operator scrambling describes how initially local operators spread under many-body dynamics and is closely connected to quantum chaos. In this work, we reveal a connection between operator scrambling and the reliability of quantum simulations. We show that the Trotter error in an observable expectation value is bounded by a scrambling correlator between the evolved observable and the multiplicative Trotter error operator. This bound retains the dependence on both the input state and the observable. We then derive entanglement-based bounds showing that sufficient entanglement brings both the observable and error-operator factors in the bound to their normalized Frobenius scales. This indicates that, for observables that are normalized sums of local Pauli terms, the leading system-size dependence of the upper bound may be reduced from O(N) to O(1) relative to the spectral-norm estimate in systems undergoing entanglement growth and quantum thermalization. Even when the evolving state is weakly entangled, the effective states generated by the observable or error operator can have larger subsystem entanglement, thereby improving the error bound. Our results clarify the fundamental connection between Trotterization, scrambling, and entanglement, and provide refined guarantees for quantum simulation of many-body dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Tianfeng Feng, Yue Cao, Qi Zhao

item.title: Observation of hysteresis in an isolated quantum system of disordered Heisenberg spins
item.description: arXiv:2508.18197v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We find energy-dependent hysteresis in an isolated Heisenberg quantum spin system, similar to thermomagnetic hysteresis in canonical spin glasses in contact with a thermal reservoir. Analogous to zero-field cooling and field cooling in conventional magnetic materials, an annealing protocol is devised to control the energy in an isolated system. Depending on the strength of disorder, the susceptibilities at zero field bifurcate at a specific energy, which signals the presence of different magnetic regimes. This behavior is apparent both in a numerical simulation by exact diagonalization of the Heisenberg Hamiltonian with twelve particles, as well as in an experiment with thousands of Rydberg atoms representing dipolar interacting quantum spins. The annealing protocols open a new path to explore the energy-dependent phase structure of spin systems at low energies. Our observation of a nonthermal metastable regime might indicate the existence of a phase transition to a novel state of isolated quantum spins.
item.dc:creator: Moritz Hornung, Eduard J. Braun, Sebastian Geier, Titus Franz, Gerhard Z\"urn, Matthias Weidem\"uller

item.title: Quantum Data Representation via Circuit Partitioning and Reintegration
item.description: arXiv:2511.05492v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum data encoding (QDE) enables faster com-putations than classical algorithms through superposition and en-tanglement. Circuit cutting and knitting are effective techniques for ameliorating current noisy quantum processing unit (QPUs) errors via a divide-and-conquer approach that splits quantum circuits into subcircuits and recombines them using classical postprocessing. Unfortunately, the existing QDE frameworks fail to consider quantum hardware limitations, such as the topology of the chip. Designing a computation model that supports the algorithm level of quantum computation and optimizes non-all-to-all connected quantum circuit simulations remains underde-veloped. In this study, we introduce shardQ, a method that leverages the SparseCut algorithm with matrix product state (MPS) compilation and a global knitting technique to mitigate the quantum error rates. This method elucidates the optimal trade-off between the computational time and error rate for quantum encoding with a theoretical proof, evidenced by an ablation analysis using an IBM Heron-type QPUs with 15% error reduction. This study also presents the results of quantum image encoding readiness. The proposed model advances the current quantum computation towards the fault-tolerant regime as QDE is the input of grand unified quantum algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Ziqing Guo, Jan Balewski, Kewen Xiao, Ziwen Pan

item.title: Statistical properties of quantum jumps between macroscopic states of light: reading an operational coherence record
item.description: arXiv:2512.07754v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose an experimental apparatus to reveal the quantum coherence manifested in downward quantum jumps of amplitude bistability. The underlying coherent superposition of macroscopic quantum states is translated into the statistical properties of the integrated charge deposited in the detector circuit of a mode-matched heterodyne/homodyne detection scheme. At first, the dynamical evolution of a signal transmitted from an auxiliary cavity is employed to pinpoint a macroscopic switching event in a bistable main cavity subject to direct photodetection. Once the decision is made on the occurrence of a downward switch, the main cavity mode is let to freely decay to the vacuum, monitored to the production of an integrated charge. In the long-time limit, the charge distribution over an identical collection of pure states generated during the jumps converges to the Q function (heterodyne detection) or marginals of the Wigner function (homodyne detection) dictated by the phase of the local oscillator. When fluctuations over the ensemble step in, we connect the statistical properties of several switching events and the ensuing production of current records, to the cavity field correlations associated with the breakdown of photon blockade.
item.dc:creator: Th. K. Mavrogordatos

item.title: Optimal Distributed Similarity Estimation of Quantum Channels
item.description: arXiv:2512.10465v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the query complexity of estimating the similarity of two unknown quantum channels available at separated devices. For channels $\mathcal{E}$ and $\mathcal{F}$ on a $d$-dimensional system, the target functional is the normalized Choi overlap ${\rm Tr}[J_{\mathcal{E}} J_{\mathcal{F}}]/d^2$, where $J_{\mathcal{E}}$ and $J_{\mathcal{F}}$ are unnormalized Choi operators. We call this task \emph{distributed similarity estimation of quantum channels} (DSEC). Our main result is a tight characterization: estimating this overlap to additive error $\varepsilon$ with constant success probability requires and is achievable with \begin{align*} \Theta\!\left(\max\left\{\frac{\sqrt d}{\varepsilon},\frac{1}{\varepsilon^2}\right\}\right) \end{align*} queries to each channel. The lower bound holds even for the most general model considered here, allowing arbitrary ancillas, coherent adaptive access, quantum memory within each laboratory, and multi-round classical communication. The dimension-dependent term follows from a shared-versus-independent Haar-unitary testing problem, while the $\varepsilon$-dependence is obtained through a random-phase channel construction. Conversely, we give a non-adaptive, ancilla-free, incoherent randomized-measurement protocol for arbitrary channels that attains the same scaling. The protocol uses only shared classical randomness to coordinate local state preparations and measurement bases. For unitary channels, our protocol reduces the dimension-dependent upper bound from $d/\varepsilon$ for independent coherent shadows to $\sqrt d/\varepsilon$. These results identify the optimal information-theoretic cost of distributed Choi overlap estimation and clarify the role of public classical randomness in distributed quantum channel learning.
item.dc:creator: Congcong Zheng, Kun Wang, Xutao Yu, Ping Xu, Zaichen Zhang

item.title: Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Composition of Quantum Circuit Optimisation Passes
item.description: arXiv:2601.21629v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many quantum software development kits provide a suite of circuit optimisation passes. These passes have been highly optimised and tested in isolation. However, the order in which they are applied is left to the user, or else defined in general-purpose default pass sequences. While general-purpose sequences miss opportunities for optimisation which are particular to individual circuits, designing pass sequences bespoke to particular circuits requires exceptional knowledge about quantum circuit design and optimisation. Here we propose and demonstrate training a reinforcement learning agent to compose optimisation-pass sequences. In particular the agent's action space consists of passes for two-qubit gate count reduction used in default PyTKET pass sequences. For the circuits in our diverse test set, the (mean, median) fraction of two-qubit gates removed by the agent is $(57.7\%, \ 56.7 \%)$, compared to $(41.8 \%, \ 50.0 \%)$ for the next best default pass sequence. In doing so our model demonstrates the ability to forgo reward to improve the final two-qubit gate count. Our approach clearly separates the problem of designing circuit optimisation passes from the problem of using them optimally in practice. We expect this separation of concerns to facilitate innovations in both areas.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Mills, Ifan Williams, Jacob Swain, Gabriel Matos, Enrico Rinaldi, Alexander Koziell-Pipe

item.title: Generating entangled polaritonic condensates by pumping with entangled pairs of photons
item.description: arXiv:2602.22778v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate the steady state of two single-mode, uniform, spatially separated polaritonic condensates exposed to resonant pumping with entangled pairs of photons in the presence of incoherent exciton reservoirs created by nonresonant optical pumping. We demonstrate the principal possibility of driving the system to an entangled state despite its exposure to noises arising from the excitonic reservoirs and photon leakage through the microcavity mirrors. We estimate the minimum pair-induced polariton influx required to drive the system into a steady state that violates the partial-transpose criterion for entanglement. Furthermore, we trace the evolution of the system after a sudden switch-off of the entangled pumping. Our analysis provides estimates for the entanglement lifetime in a system of two exciton-polariton condensates.
item.dc:creator: N. A. Asriyan, A. A. Elistratov, A. V. Kavokin

item.title: Dequantization Barriers for Guided Stoquastic Hamiltonians
item.description: arXiv:2602.23183v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We construct a probability distribution, induced by the Perron--Frobenius eigenvector of an exponentially large graph, that cannot be efficiently sampled by any classical algorithm, even when given the best-possible warm-start distribution. In the quantum setting, this problem can be viewed as preparing the ground state of a stoquastic Hamiltonian given a guiding state as input, and is known to be efficiently solvable on a quantum computer. We further show that even estimating the ground-state energy of that Hamiltonian remains classically hard. Our results suggest that no efficient classical algorithm can solve a broad class of stoquastic ground-state problems. Our graph is constructed from a class of high-degree, high-girth spectral expanders (such as the LPS Ramanujan graphs) to which self-similar trees are attached. This builds on and extends prior work of Gily\'en, Hastings, and Vazirani (Quantum 2021, STOC 2021), which ruled out dequantization for a specific stoquastic adiabatic path algorithm. We strengthen their result by ruling out any classical algorithm for guided ground-state preparation or energy estimation, while also providing a derandomized construction.
item.dc:creator: Yassine Hamoudi, Yvan Le Borgne, Shrinidhi Teganahally Sridhara

item.title: Quantum Theory Over Dual-Complex Numbers
item.description: arXiv:2603.17581v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We take quantum theory and replace C by C[e] where e^2 = 0, i.e. we extend quantum theory to the ring of dual complex numbers. The aim is to develop a common language in which to treat continuous quantum physics and discrete quantum models in a unified manner, including their symmetries. Since quantum theory is linear, introducing e is enough to model infinitesimals. A first objection to this programme is that C[e] is not a field, since division by e is undefined, while quantum mechanics typically relies on division. A second objection concerns whether unitarity still makes sense given e^2 = 0. Hence, the core of this work is dedicated to proving that dual-complex quantum theory remains fully consistent. In particular, norm is preserved at all times, and renormalization never requires dividing by an infinitesimal. An equivalence with conventional quantum theory is demonstrated: the dual-complex extension of a parametrized quantum operation automatically provides a linear treatment of its first-order variations. As a first example application, we provide a unified description of both the Dirac equation in the continuum and the Dirac Quantum Walk in the discrete. We establish the discrete Lorentz covariance of the latter.
item.dc:creator: Nathan Houyet (\'Ecole Normale Sup\'erieure de Paris-Saclay), Dogukan Bakircioglu (Universit\'e Paris-Saclay, Inria, CNRS, LMF), Pablo Arrighi (Universit\'e Paris-Saclay, Inria, CNRS, LMF)

item.title: Using spatiotemporal Born rule for testing macroscopic realism
item.description: arXiv:2603.21793v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show that, given an evolving quantum system and the quasiprobability distribution generated by the spatiotemporal generalization of the Born rule in pseudo-density matrices (PDMs), this distribution deviates from the sequential measurement probability distribution, given by the L\"uders-von Neumann distribution, if and only if the non-signaling in time is violated; therefore, macroscopic realism can be tested using the spatiotemporal Born rule. Furthermore, we study a definition of temporal entanglement according to the structure of the PDMs that is analogous to the definition of spatial entanglement in density matrices, and we employ our results to explore the relationship between the negativity of the PDM, temporal entanglement, violation of temporal Bell inequalities, and macroscopic realism. From the examples, a clear distinction between violation of macroscopic realism and of temporal Bell inequalities is made, as well as simple examples where a clear causal witness is present while non-signaling in time and macroscopic realism are respected.
item.dc:creator: Naim Elias Comar, Lucas C. C\'eleri, Mia Stamatova, Vlatko Vedral, Aditya Varna Iyer, Rafael Chaves

item.title: SesQ: A Surface Electrostatic Simulator for Precise Energy Participation Ratio Simulation in Superconducting Qubits
item.description: arXiv:2603.28524v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An accurate and efficient numerical electromagnetic model for superconducting qubits is essential for characterizing and minimizing design-dependent dielectric losses. The energy participation ratio (EPR) is the commonly adopted metric used to evaluate these losses, but its calculation presents a severe multiscale computational challenge. Conventional finite element method (FEM) requires 3D volumetric meshing, leading to prohibitive computational costs and memory requirements when attempting to capture singular electric fields at nanometer-thin material interfaces. To address this bottleneck, we propose SesQ, a surface integral equation simulator tailored for the precise simulation of the EPR. By applying discretization on 2D surfaces, deriving a semi-analytical multilayer Green's function, and employing a dedicated non-conformal boundary mesh refinement scheme, SesQ accurately resolves singular edge fields without an explosive growth in the number of unknowns. Validations with analytically solvable models demonstrate that SesQ accelerates capacitance extraction by roughly two orders of magnitude compared to commercial FEM tools. While achieving comparable accuracy for capacitance extraction, SesQ delivers superior precision for EPR calculation. Simulations of practical transmon qubits further reveal that FEM approaches tend to significantly underestimate the EPR. Finally, the high efficiency of SesQ enables rapid iteration in the layout optimization, as demonstrated by minimizing the EPR of the qubit pattern, establishing the simulator as a powerful tool for the automated design of low-loss superconducting quantum circuits.
item.dc:creator: Ziang Wang, Shuyuan Guan, Feng Wu, Xiaohang Zhang, Qiong Li, Jianxin Chen, Xin Wan, Tian Xia, Hui-Hai Zhao

item.title: Probes of chaos over the Clifford group and approach to Haar values
item.description: arXiv:2603.29695v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Chaotic behavior of quantum systems can be characterized by the adherence of the expectation values of given probes to moments of the Haar distribution. In this work, we analyze the behavior of several probes of chaos using a technique known as Isospectral Twirling [1]. This consists in fixing the spectrum of the Hamiltonian and picking its eigenvectors at random. Here, we study the transition from stabilizer bases to random bases according to the Haar measure by T-doped random quantum circuits. We then compute the average value of the probes over ensembles of random spectra from Random Matrix Theory, the Gaussian Diagonal Ensemble and the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble, associated with non-chaotic and chaotic behavior respectively. We also study the behavior of such probes over the Toric Code Hamiltonian.
item.dc:creator: Stefano Cusumano, Gianluca Esposito, Alioscia Hamma

item.title: On the Computational Power of Geometrically Local QAC circuits
item.description: arXiv:2604.07178v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The computational power of $\mathsf{QAC}$, which are constant-depth quantum circuit families consisting of arbitrary single-qubit unitaries and n-qubit generalized Toffoli gates, has gained tremendous focus recently. In this work, we initiate the study of the computational complexity of geometrically local $\mathsf{QAC}$ circuits, where the qubits are arranged in a high-dimensional grid, and all the generalized Toffoli gates act on contiguous qubits along one direction. We prove that $\mathsf{2D\text{-}QAC}$ circuits are universal: any $\mathsf{QAC}$ circuit can be exactly simulated by a two-dimensional geometrically local $\mathsf{QAC}$ circuit. Therefore, we focus on the computational power of $\mathsf{2D\text{-}QAC}$ circuits with grid width $w$. We prove that $\mathsf{PARITY}$ computation has a tight width--depth tradeoff of $w=n^{\Theta(1/d)}$ in the constant-depth regime if the circuit allows arbitrary ancilla. Moreover, for polynomial-size circuits, a width lower bound of $n^{\omega(1/d)}$ for $\mathsf{PARITY}$ would imply $\mathsf{PARITY}\notin\mathsf{QAC}^0$. We also establish Fourier tail and sensitivity bounds, together with tight width lower bounds and tight depth lower bounds in $\mathsf{1D\text{-}QAC}$ circuits for $\mathsf{MAJORITY}$ and $\mathsf{MOD}$ computation. Our main tool is \emph{local measurement variance}, the maximum variance of normalized sums of observables on separated regions. We use a hybrid argument to show that each layer of a $\mathsf{2D\text{-}QAC}^0$ circuit increases this variance by at most a factor depending only on its width, yielding a variance bound for every $\mathsf{2D\text{-}QAC}^0$ state. The high local measurement variance of cat and Dicke states then gives the width lower bounds.
item.dc:creator: Yangjing Dong, Fengning Ou, Penghui Yao

item.title: Quantum Kicked Top: A Paradigmatic Model
item.description: arXiv:2604.12345v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The quantum kicked top (QKT) is one of the most widely studied models in quantum chaos, providing a minimal yet powerful framework for exploring the relationship between classical nonlinear dynamics and quantum behavior. Unlike many chaotic systems with infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, the QKT possesses a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, making it analytically and numerically controllable while still showing a rich dynamical phenomena. In this chapter, we present a comprehensive introduction to the QKT as a paradigmatic model of quantum chaos. Starting from the classical kicked top, we derive the discrete nonlinear map governing the dynamics on the unit sphere and analyze its phase space structure through fixed points, stability analysis, bifurcations and Lyapunov exponents. We then discuss the role of symmetries, including rotational and time-reversal symmetry, and how their breaking modifies the dynamics. The quantum description is developed using Floquet theory, where the periodically driven spin system is represented by a unitary Floquet operator acting on a $(2j+1)$-dimensional Hilbert space. Within this framework, signatures of quantum chaos such as spectral statistics, entanglement generation and recurrences are discussed. The model also admits an interpretation as a system of interacting qubits, enabling explicit few-qubit realizations and direct connections with quantum information measures through reduced density matrices and entanglement entropy. By linking classical phase space structures with quantum dynamical indicators, the QKT provides a clear setting to investigate the emergence of chaotic behavior in the semiclassical limit. The chapter, therefore, highlights the quantum kicked top as a bridge between nonlinear classical dynamics, quantum chaos and modern quantum information science.
item.dc:creator: Avadhut V. Purohit, Udaysinh T. Bhosale

item.title: High-performance cellular automaton decoders for quantum repetition and toric code
item.description: arXiv:2604.21866v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Execution of quantum algorithms on large-scale quantum computers will require extremely low logical error rates and scalable decoding architectures. Local decoders are promising candidates for this task because they avoid the communication and data-processing bottlenecks inherent in global decoding strategies. Here, we present SCALA (Signaling CA with Local Attraction), a non-hierarchical cellular automaton decoder for quantum repetition and toric codes, and compare it with the hierarchical CA decoder proposed by Harrington. SCALA combines constant local memory and simple nearest-neighbor signaling with a system-size-dependent global reset schedule. We find a code-capacity threshold estimate of $p_c\simeq7.40(5)\%$ and sub-threshold scaling approaching $p_L\propto p^{d/4}$ for the toric code. For the finite system sizes accessible numerically, and despite numerical evidence for the absence of a finite critical threshold, SCALA also provides strong logical-error suppression under phenomenological noise while retaining its low local computational overhead. SCALA furthermore remains robust when its internal signals are themselves noisy. Together with its simple local dynamics, this makes SCALA particularly interesting for low-overhead real-time decoding and motivates its exploration as a quantum cellular automaton for measurement-free quantum error correction.
item.dc:creator: Don Winter, Thiago L. M. Guedes, Markus M\"uller

item.title: General method for obtaining the energy minimum of spin Hamiltonians for separable states
item.description: arXiv:2605.03022v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce a highly general method to determine the energy minimum of spin Hamiltonians over separable states when the single-particle reduced density matrices are fixed. We present efficient numerical methods that reduce the problem to calculations in a two-particle system. For a broad class of very general spin models, we present analytic formulas for the minimum. For ferromagnetic Ising and Ising-like models of spin-j particles, the minimum over separable states on two-colorable lattices, and over symmetric separable states on fully connected graphs, is given by a compact analytic formula involving the quantum Fisher information. For antiferromagnetic Ising-like and XY-like models of spin j-particles living on a complete graph, the energy minimum for symmetric separable states is given with the expectation value of single-particle operators. For the ferromagnetic Heisenberg chain of spin-1/2 particles, the minimum is expressed via the Uhlmann-Jozsa fidelity. These relations enable the extraction of the quantum Fisher information and quantum fidelity of the corresponding single-particle reduced states from correlation measurements on ground-state ensembles of suitably engineered spin models. For a number of other models, we obtain not necessarily tight lower bounds. We also present bounds for various levels of multiparticle entanglement.
item.dc:creator: G\'eza T\'oth, J\'ozsef Pitrik

item.title: Efficient Multi-Controlled Gate Implementation in Trapped-Ion Systems
item.description: arXiv:2605.04654v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-controlled gates are essential primitives in quantum algorithms, yet implementing them via standard gate-level decompositions remains resource-intensive. We develop efficient pulse-level implementations of multi-controlled gates in trapped-ion systems using the Cirac-Zoller scheme. We first show that the Cirac-Zoller construction admits a freedom in the sign choice of red-sideband (RSB) pulses, which leaves the logical operation invariant up to a local Pauli-$Z$ correction. By exploiting this freedom, we construct equivalent realizations of multi-controlled gates and develop pulse cancellation for more efficient implementations of successive gates. We perform numerical simulations and show that pulse cancellation reduces the gate time and improves the state fidelity. Furthermore, we propose ancilla-free circuits for general $N$-controlled gates that use a single-controlled gate primitive and $\mathcal{O}(N)$ RSB pulses. As a key application, we apply our pulse cancellation to the linear combination of unitaries (LCU) method for block encoding. We show that the RSB-pulse cost of the select operator over $L$ unitaries can be reduced from $\mathcal{O}(L\log L)$ to $\mathcal{O}(L)$, which improves the efficiency and scalability of LCU-based quantum circuits.
item.dc:creator: Minhyeok Kang, Taejin Kim, Jungsoo Hong, Joonsuk Huh

item.title: Computational and physical complexity of synthesizing random multi-qudit quantum states and unitary operators
item.description: arXiv:2605.07374v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We analyze the complexity of synthesizing random states and unitary operators in a multi-qudit system in two paradigms. In one case, we consider the situation in which we manipulate the system by applying a sequence of one- and two-qudit quantum gates that constitute the elementary, and universal, gate set. The minimum number of gates required to perform the desired operation represents the computational complexity. In the other case, we consider the situation in which we manipulate the physical system using physical fields with optimized control pulses. The minimum time required to perform the desired operation represents the physical complexity. In both cases, we use analytical arguments in combination with optimal-control-theory numerical calculations to determine the complexity of random operations. We show analytically that the computational complexity of synthesizing random states or unitary operators scales exponentially with the number of qudits. While our numerical results are limited to small systems and are insufficient to reveal the asymptotic scaling laws, they suggest that the physical complexity of synthesizing random quantum states and unitary operators scales more slowly than the computational complexity. We discuss various implications of our results, especially concerning the relationship between random and pseudorandom states and unitary operators.
item.dc:creator: Sahel Ashhab, Bora Basyildiz

item.title: Quantum Trajectories: Ergodicity, Perturbative Dynamics, and Stationary Response
item.description: arXiv:2606.13470v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum trajectories capture measurement-conditioned statistics beyond ensemble averages. For finite-dimensional Kraus dynamics, complete-reset and overlap conditions yield a unique invariant law with explicit geometric total-variation contraction. Under finite-reference mixing and quantitative transverse contraction, $C^2$ Kraus perturbations yield two complementary stationary limits: an affine tangent law for local fluctuations and an occupation measure for rare excursions. These limits give leading observable-response formulas, including an excursion contribution at quadratic order; both limits and coefficients depend only on reference Kraus operators and their first derivatives. For Clifford-driven monitored trajectories, group structure verifies the general hypotheses and yields geometric Wasserstein mixing uniformly over intermediate unitaries at fixed dimensions, an equivalence between uniform total-variation ergodicity and a finite nonzero rank-one Kraus product for each fixed unitary, and exact stationary tangent energies. Under partial measurement, tangent dynamics have almost surely finite memory with a sharp exponential tail; every $C^2$ state observable has vanishing first-order stationary response. For weak Hamiltonian perturbations, odd-prime Gross--Wigner mana responds linearly in the perturbation strength $\theta$, whereas prime-dimensional stabilizer R\'enyi entropies scale as $\theta^{2\alpha}$, $\theta^2\ln(1/\theta)$, and $\theta^2$ for fixed $0<\alpha<1$, $\alpha=1$, and $1<\alpha<\infty$, respectively. Under partial measurement, the leading coefficients are strictly positive precisely for Hamiltonians outside the real span of the measurement projectors; on this quotient, the mana coefficient defines a norm and the order-one logarithmic coefficient an explicit positive-definite quadratic form.
item.dc:creator: Guocheng Zhen, Xuanrong Yang, Chengkai Zhu, Ranyiliu Chen, Xin Wang

item.title: Generic Number-of-Copies Amplification for Pseudorandom States
item.description: arXiv:2606.29325v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show that any quantum pseudorandom state that is secure against single-copy distinguishers, i.e. a $1$-PRS, can be amplified to $t$-copy security, i.e. to a $t$-PRS, without additional assumptions, for any polynomial $t$ in the security parameter. Prior work (Ananth and Goldin, CRYPTO 2026) was only able to show this for a restricted class of $1$-PRS constructions, namely ones whose generators only use a small number of ancilla qubits. Technically, we show that by carefully accounting for the randomness that is used in the construction, and using quantum extractors, it is possible to eliminate an ancilla register of any length and obtain a meaningful $t$-PRS outcome.
item.dc:creator: Zvika Brakerski, Miri Zenilman

item.title: BRIDGE: Lazy-Move Compilation for Dual-Species Neutral-Atom Quantum Computers
item.description: arXiv:2606.31833v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Neutral-atom quantum computers commonly connect distant qubits by transporting atoms, incurring trap-handover errors, heating, and atom loss. We present BRIDGE (Buffer-Relay Interconnect for Data-stable Gate Execution), a hardware--software co-design that connects stationary data atoms through a fixed, second-species buffer network. Short buffer chains mediate remote controlled-Z gates and return to their initial states after each operation. BRIDGE-F combines relay routing with buffer-mediated SWAPs to relocate quantum states without transporting atoms. BRIDGE-H additionally permits data-atom transport when its full modeled cost is offset by higher survival-weighted fidelity. Across 21 circuits, BRIDGE-F exceeds ZAP and Enola in modeled survival-weighted fidelity, with geometric-mean ratios of $2.1\times$ and $38\times$ and medians of $1.3\times$ and $3.7\times$. Modeled execution latency is lower by factors of approximately $500$ and $1{,}350$, respectively, with circuit single-qubit costs excluded and relay/SWAP Hadamards included. On the same fabric, BRIDGE-F matches or exceeds SABRE-based routing on 17 circuits. Rescoring nominal plans with relay-module error equal to direct-CZ error preserves the advantage over ZAP across all 21 circuits, although recompilation can underperform on QFT. These results identify stationary buffer-mediated connectivity as a promising alternative to repeated atom transport under the stated physical assumptions.
item.dc:creator: Chen Huang, Jingbo Wang, Zhemin Zhang, Ming Zhong, Zhuo Fu, Zhiding Liang, Yuan Sun, Dong E. Liu

item.title: Quantum Channel Polynomial Processing
item.description: arXiv:2607.06557v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce a quantum algorithmic framework based on probabilistic mixtures of unitary channels that, similar to the framework of quantum singular value transformations, enables the application of arbitrary polynomials of hermitian operators onto arbitrary initial states. We show that our framework supports a flexible tradeoff between sample- and query complexity ranging from optimal query complexity, meaning logarithmic in the error, and exponentially scaling sample complexity to sub-polynomial query complexity in the error and polynomial sample complexity. Combined with the considerably lower quantum circuit complexity, compared to quantum singular value transformations with a linear combination of unitaries block encoding, we argue that our framework can be seamlessly scaled from NISQ to fault-tolerant quantum computing.
item.dc:creator: Tianhan Liu, Fedor Simkovic IV, Martin Leib

item.title: A hardware-efficient variational ansatz with an exact diagonal metric for real- and imaginary-time evolution and Haar sampling
item.description: arXiv:2607.07942v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Variational quantum algorithms depend on the geometry of their parametrised circuits: metric-aware optimisation and time evolution require the Fubini--Study metric, which has hitherto demanded costly auxiliary measurements and ill-conditioned inversions. This work introduces a hardware-efficient $n$-qubit ansatz, which parametrises states by a binary tree and whose Hilbert-space pullback metric is diagonal in closed form. Quantum natural gradient on the tree parameters, variational imaginary- and real-time evolution, and exact unitary-invariant (Haar) sampling on a symmetry sector run with no auxiliary metric circuits or matrix inversion. When the target state is supported on a subspace of $k$ computational-basis states, the redundant tree parameters carry a gauge freedom a pruning compiler converts into circuits whose two-qubit count provably grows linearly in $k$; a variant reaches near-optimal $O(nk/\log n)$ scaling with the closed-form metric intact. On electronic-structure calculations for small molecules and half-filled Hubbard quench dynamics, the method reaches reference-level accuracy with one to three orders of magnitude fewer two-qubit gates than leading alternatives. Interchangeable constructions (a Schur-transform dressing or internal reparameterisations) make the ansatz exactly spin-adapted, with fixed total spin at every parameter and no penalty terms. The bare ansatz is an exactly controllable, well-conditioned and barren-plateau-free primitive for preparing and sampling sector states: on its own, it is classically simulable in $k$ (a boundary proved for a general class of sector-sparse ans\"atze); composed with a classically hard dressing, it yields molecular ground states, sector-Haar benchmarking, thermal correlators, and exact effective Hamiltonians trained from energy measurements alone, with the composed circuit carrying the potential for quantum advantage.
item.dc:creator: Dario Picozzi

item.title: Saturating the Bayesian Nagaoka-Hayashi bound within numerical precision for the depolarization SU(2) rotation channel
item.description: arXiv:2607.15398v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Bayesian Nagaoka--Hayashi (NH) bound is a semidefinite lower bound on the Bayes risk of multiparameter estimation, tighter than the Bayesian symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD) Cramer--Rao bounds, and whether it can be attained is an open problem. We study the single-shot estimation of a qubit rotation, all three parameters at once, under depolarizing noise and a uniform prior, with k parallel uses of the channel. Rotational covariance reduces the joint optimization of probe, measurement, and estimator, and the NH bound itself, to small semidefinite programs, solvable through k=4. At every number of uses and noise strength the optimized strategy reaches the NH bound within the numerical precision of the calculation, numerical evidence that the bound is attained for this channel family, while the SLD bound lies strictly below and is never attained. As the noise grows the optimal probe collapses to the tensored Bell state.
item.dc:creator: Leo Bia, Christos N. Gagatsos

item.title: Security of quantum key distribution with passive basis choice and detection-efficiency mismatch for a realistic satellite setup
item.description: arXiv:2608.09793v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Detection efficiency mismatch is a common problem in realistic quantum key distribution (QKD) systems. Existing security proofs for passive basis choice provide a nonzero secret key rate for small detection efficiency mismatches only. Unfortunately, in realistic setups, the detection efficiency mismatch can be significant. Here, we present a different approach for estimating the secret key rate for the BB84 protocol with passive basis choice and a detection efficiency mismatch between four threshold detectors, where the mismatch is not assumed to be small. We also adapt the decoy-state method for this case. The suggested approach is used to estimate the secret key rate in a QKD experiment between the Micius satellite and the Zvenigorod ground station.
item.dc:creator: Egor Ivchenko, Aleksandr Khmelev, Vladimir Kurochkin, Anton Trushechkin

item.title: Negative quasiprobability trajectories for Bell-diagonal states under local decoherence
item.description: arXiv:2608.16358v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The fluctuation theorem (FT) relates microscopic trajectory distributions to macroscopic averages. Using quasiprobability trajectories, this framework has recently been extended to quantum information dynamics. Despite sharing the form of conventional thermodynamic FTs, information FTs involve quasiprobabilities whose negativity and statistical properties remain poorly understood. In this work, we analytically determine the properties of negative distributions for two-qubit Bell-diagonal states evolving under local dephasing, depolarizing, and amplitude-damping channels, under the fixed local computational basis. We show that the occurrence of negative quasiprobabilities is not determined by the entanglement or Bell nonlocality of the initial state. For these channels, a diagonal-interference decomposition identifies a nonnegative reference contribution and yields channel-dependent interference bounds. More importantly, we prove that quasiprobability distributions containing negative weights can violate Horv\'ath's necessary and sufficient criterion for the Jensen-Steffensen inequality to hold for every continuous convex function, even though the specific exponential Jensen-like relation enforced by the FT and the quantum data-processing inequality remains valid. This trajectory-level contrast with classical stochastic descriptions reveals a distinctive feature of quantum information dynamics that is invisible when only the corresponding average-level information inequalities are considered.
item.dc:creator: Qing Yu, Kun Zhang, Yang-Yang Chen, Xiao-Hui Wang

item.title: On the geometry, typicality, and detectability of quantum magic
item.description: arXiv:2609.03944v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum magic, or nonstabilizerness, is a central resource for quantum computation, motivating a systematic study of its mathematical structure and physical behavior. Here we characterize the geometry of the stabilizer polytope, obtaining near-tight bounds on its inradius, volume radius, and number of facets. These results reveal a pronounced separation between the typical presence of magic and its detectability. In particular, random mixed states obtained by tracing out an environment remain magical with high probability even when the environment contains nearly twice as many qubits as the system, demonstrating parametrically greater robustness to environmental mixing than bipartite entanglement. In contrast, commonly used magic criteria, including the Triangle and Pauli-norm-based criteria, lose detection power under much weaker mixing. More generally, when the number of environment qubits scales proportionally with the system size, certification with constant success probability requires exponentially many linear observables, even given their exact expectation values. We also prove that the number of facets of the stabilizer polytope grows doubly exponentially with the number of qubits, making exhaustive witness enumeration impractical for complete magic certification and motivating approaches that exploit the structure and symmetries of stabilizer states.
item.dc:creator: Zhenhuan Liu, Zi-Wen Liu

item.title: Lee-Yang theorem for fermions
item.description: arXiv:2609.23942v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Lee-Yang theorems are a powerful tool for studying many-body systems, with applications ranging from analyzing phase transitions to proving the efficiency of certain classical and quantum algorithms. In this work, we prove a Lee-Yang zero-freeness theorem for the partition function of a broad class of interacting fermion models, implying the existence of a provably efficient quantum algorithm for estimating their ground-state energies. This class includes several well-known models such as the attractive Hubbard model, repulsive Hubbard model on bipartite graphs, and the interacting Hofstadter model. Our results also rigorously establish the nonexistence of phase transitions in these models in the presence of a nonzero local external field.
item.dc:creator: Chaithanya Rayudu, Takahiro Misawa, Andrew Zhao, Jun Takahashi

item.title: Exact Gaussian Entanglement Dynamics and Initial-State Control in Coupled Parametric Oscillators
item.description: arXiv:2609.32709v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study two bilinearly coupled harmonic oscillators driven by a common time-dependent spring. A fixed normal-mode transformation reduces the pair to two parametric oscillators, each solved exactly by its Lewis-Riesenfeld invariant and Ermakov-Pinney amplitude, including the ladder-operator construction and the Lewis-Riesenfeld phase. For invariant-vacuum inputs the physical two-mode covariance matrix is obtained in closed form, and the logarithmic negativity collapses to $E_{N}=\frac{1}{2} \operatorname{arcosh}(X/2)$, where a single dimensionless invariant $X \geq 2$ measures the relative phase-space deformation of the two normal modes. We give a normalization-explicit account of the Duan--Simon comparison: after local symplectic optimization the Duan test and the positive partial transpose share the entanglement threshold for this pure exchange-symmetric Gaussian family, but the optimized Duan quantity is a witness, not an independent measure, with $D_{\rm opt}/D_{\rm sep}=e^{-E_N}$. We carefully separate a genuinely separable product preparation from the already-entangled ground state of the coupled Hamiltonian, and use only the former for claims of entanglement generation. Under sinusoidal stiffness modulation a separable input shows bounded correlations away from resonance and sustained growth near parametric resonance, and we demonstrate numerically that the initial width and chirp act as two independent, experimentally accessible controls of the entanglement at a chosen target time. An $SU(1,1)$ formulation identifies $2 E_{N}$ with the hyperbolic separation of the two normal-mode squeezing trajectories on the $SU(1,1)/U(1)$ disk and shows that entanglement is governed by both the relative squeezing magnitude and the relative squeezing angle; ; we exhibit regimes in which nearly equal magnitudes still produce strong entanglement through the angle alone.
item.dc:creator: Roberto Bernal-Jaquez, Hector H. Hernandez-Hernandez, Alexander Schaum, Guillermo Chacon-Acosta

item.title: Induced Coherence in Quantum and Classical Interferometry: Origin and Control
item.description: arXiv:2609.35523v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The wave-particle duality that manifests in Young's double-slit interferometry satisfying the well known Englert-Greenberger-Yasin inequality has been shown to obey a universal triality relation involving coherence, predictability and rather surprisingly entanglement. In the present work, we explicitly demonstrate the persistence of the triality relation in the quantum induced coherence interferometer and the classical configuration recovers the well known duality inequality. Furthermore, we explore the origin of coherence and entanglement, in the induced coherence interferometer, and means to control them. We show that path indistinguishability (or intrinsic indistinguishability of the sources) in our setup plays a complementary role in influencing both interference and entanglement. We bring out manifestly the nature of coherence in both classical and quantum versions of induced coherence interferometers.
item.dc:creator: Balakrishnan Viswanathan, Ravi Kamal Pandey, Leena Barshilia, Devendra Kumar Mishra, Sibasish Ghosh, Prasanta K. Panigrahi

item.title: Leakage suppression for high-fidelity exchange gates and quantum simulation in superconducting circuits
item.description: arXiv:2609.37296v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Parametric frequency modulation makes superconducting interactions programmable for quantum gates and quantum simulation. Leakage into higher transmon levels and coupler modes degrades gate fidelity and takes simulated dynamics outside the intended state space. Simple pulse shaping reduces off-resonant excitation, while strong coupling and short pulses demand simultaneous control of multiple leakage pathways. Controlling these pathways across individual exchange operations and simultaneous couplings is essential for fast gates and faithful programmable dynamics. We introduce parametric derivative removal by adiabatic gate (PDRAG), combining derivative shaping and finite-pulse calibration for qubit and coupler modulation. At an interqubit coupling of $g/2\pi=100$ MHz, simulations demonstrate 13-ns exchange operations, approaching the timescale of fast single-qubit gates. Combined with calibrated phase accumulation, these pulses realize a two-parameter fSim gate family with infidelity below $1.8\times10^{-7}$. For quantum simulation, PDRAG suppresses leakage and improves fidelity in continuous and digital Floquet simulations of Su--Schrieffer--Heeger chains. Floquet analysis identifies finite-pulse return interference as the calibration mechanism; realistic-circuit transfer preserves suppression. PDRAG establishes a unified framework spanning quantum gates and quantum simulation.
item.dc:creator: Yiwen Li, Xinsheng Tan, Yang Yu

item.title: Optimal Quantum Junta Testing
item.description: arXiv:2609.37926v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We determine the quantum query complexity of testing $k$-juntas for Boolean functions, unitaries, and quantum channels. Let $n$ denote the number of input bits or qubits and $\varepsilon$ the distance parameter. For all sufficiently large $k$, $n \ge 2k$, and $2^{-k/16} \le \varepsilon \le 1/16$, we establish the following tight bounds. $\bullet$ Junta functions: The query complexity is $\Theta(\sqrt{k/\varepsilon})$, closing the gap left by Ambainis, Belovs, Regev, and de Wolf (SODA 2016) and Bun, Kothari, and Thaler (STOC 2018, ToC 2020). $\bullet$ Junta unitaries: The query complexity is $\Theta(\sqrt{k}/\varepsilon)$, closing the gap left by Chen, Nadimpalli, and Yuen (SODA 2023). With forward-only access, the query complexity is $\Theta(k/(\varepsilon^2 \log k))$. At constant $\varepsilon$, these bounds establish a separation between $\Theta(\sqrt{k})$ queries with forward and inverse access and $\Theta(k/\log k)$ queries with forward-only access. $\bullet$ Junta channels: The query complexity is $\Theta(k/(\varepsilon^2 \log k))$, closing the gap left by Bao and Yao (COLT 2023, TPAMI 2025). The upper bounds for channels and forward-only unitaries are achieved by nonadaptive, ancilla-free testers using product inputs and single-qubit measurements. Our upper bounds follow from a reduction to \emph{union size testing}, a generalization of support size testing to distributions over subsets of a ground set. We develop optimal testers for this problem both from independent samples and from a reversible sampler. Our matching lower bounds use moment-matching constructions and a phase-masked unitary ensemble. For this ensemble, the average acceptance probability of every forward-only quantum algorithm admits an exact representation in terms of independent classical samples.
item.dc:creator: Jinge Bao, Minbo Gao, Penghui Yao

item.title: A Dichotomy for MIP* in the Presence of Unital Noise
item.description: arXiv:2609.39318v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study two-prover one-round quantum interactive proofs in which the provers share arbitrarily many copies of a noisy EPR pair. Prior work showed that if the shared state $\psi$ has quantum maximal correlation $\rho_{\max}(\psi) < 1$, then $\mathrm{MIP}^{\psi}[\mathrm{poly}, O(1)] = \mathrm{MIP} = \mathrm{NEXP}$, while noiseless EPR pairs give $\mathrm{MIP}^{\mathrm{EPR}}[\mathrm{poly}, O(1)] = \mathrm{RE}$. That result leaves two cases open: answers of polynomial length, and noise that keeps $\rho_{\max}(\psi) = 1$, which unital noise can do. We settle both for unital noise. Equivalently, let $\psi$ be any two-qubit state with maximally mixed marginals. We show that $$\mathsf{MIP}^{\psi}[\mathrm{poly},\mathrm{poly}] =\mathsf{MIP} =\mathsf{NEXP},~\text{if $\psi$ is separable or $\rho_{\max}(\psi)<1$};$$ $$\mathsf{MIP}^{\psi}[\mathrm{poly},\mathrm{poly}] =\mathsf{RE}, \text{if $\psi$ is entangled and $\rho_{\max}(\psi)=1$.}$$ Beyond this complexity-theoretic dichotomy, our proof introduces two techniques of potential independent interest. The first technique approximates quantum measurements by positive low-degree operators. We prove that the square roots of the measurement elements, after applying the smoothing operation, can be approximated by low-degree operators, with error controlled in the Schatten 4-norm. This further gives a positive low-degree approximation with small normalization error. Second, we introduce Pauli folding, a randomized dimension-reduction method for low-degree quantum operators. For fixed accuracy, the number of qubits after folding is polynomial in the Pauli degree and the number of outcomes and does not depend on $n$. Moreover, Pauli folding preserves Hilbert-Schmidt inner products in expectation and is approximately multiplicative. This is an exponential improvement over the dimension reductions via invariance principles in all previous works.
item.dc:creator: Yangjing Dong, Zhenyu Jiang, Minglong Qin, Penghui Yao, Haigang Zhou

item.title: Dissipation accelerates quantum and classical simulation of open-system dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2609.40174v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Simulating open quantum systems reveals how environmental coupling shapes relaxation, excitation transport, and the dynamics of quantum correlations. On quantum hardware, dissipative channels add operations and might seem to increase cost. However, we show that a broad class of Pauli noise, including depolarization, can ease quantum and classical simulation by exponentially suppressing high-weight components of Heisenberg-evolved observables. For bounded-degree Lindblad dynamics, this permits system-size-independent Trotter steps when estimating local observables. Combining this compression with Richardson extrapolation, we provide classical and quantum error bounds with respect to the 2-norm of the propagated observable. These give high-probability expectation-value guarantees for random input states or random Hamiltonians acting on a fixed state and control (out-of-time-order) correlators. Concretely, we show that expectation values of local observables at time $t$ can be estimated to accuracy $\varepsilon$ using circuits of maximum depth $O\!\left(\left[1+\left(t/\gamma\right)^{3/2}\right]\log^2(1/\varepsilon)\right)$, independent of the system size $n$. Classically, we show that sparse Pauli propagation runs in time polynomial in $n$, $t$ and $1/\varepsilon$ for every fixed $\gamma>0$, with polynomial degree $O(1/\gamma)$ in the weak dissipation limit. The gap between our quantum and classical upper bounds leaves room for a substantial polynomial quantum advantage as dissipation weakens, an observation further supported by our numerical results.
item.dc:creator: Armando Angrisani, Ricard Puig, Yanting Teng, Zo\"{e} Holmes

item.title: Strong Simulation of 1D Quantum Circuits via Reduced Transition Matrices
item.description: arXiv:2610.02082v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Tensor networks are powerful tools for simulating quantum many-body systems, but the growth of spatial entanglement severely limits the direct evolution of pure states under chaotic unitary circuits. Here we address the task of evaluating specified output probabilities of one-dimensional circuits at finite relative precision. We introduce a sweeping algorithm that contracts the circuit transversely and compresses its two temporal boundaries jointly through reduced transition matrices (RTMs), preserving their overlap rather than either boundary separately. At fixed target precision, the retained bond dimension exhibits a slowdown consistent with subexponential growth over the accessible time window, in a regime where the circuit is already deeply anticoncentrated. A noisy random-operator model illustrates how finite precision can induce a crossover from linear to logarithmic temporal entropy growth. These results open a route to probability queries for benchmarking and learning without representing the full quantum state.
item.dc:creator: Matilde Grassi, Stefano Carignano, Luca Tagliacozzo, Jacopo De Nardis

item.title: Polynomial-Time Algorithms for Nuclear Tensor Norms and Multipartite Quantum Separability
item.description: arXiv:2610.03637v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study a multilinear optimization problem for tensors with bounded Frobenius norm, where each of the $k$ local factors of dimension $d$ is chosen from a convex set. We give a deterministic algorithm running in time $d^{O(k)}$ for constant additive approximations. As applications, we obtain the first polynomial-time algorithms at constant accuracy for weak membership in the nuclear-norm unit ball of high-order tensors and for multipartite quantum separability in Frobenius norm. Our approach views tensor optimization as a cooperative multiprover game and combines this perspective with a recursive spectral compression procedure. We then show that related ideas admit a quantum implementation when the input state is given through copies, rather than an explicit classical description. In this setting, we obtain an algorithm to solve Frobenius-norm separability testing using $\text{poly}(k)$ copies and $\text{poly}(k\log d)$ time.
item.dc:creator: Martino Bernasconi, Giulio Malavolta

item.title: Non-Orthogonal Amplitude Amplification for Hybrid CV-DV Quantum Processors
item.description: arXiv:2610.09353v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce a non-orthogonal amplitude amplification (NOAA) method for hybrid continuous-variable- discrete-variable (CV-DV) quantum processors, where the available CV-assisted projector is not perfectly se- lective for the target state. We establish a bound on the achievable target-state fidelity, which is determined by the initial target-state amplitude and the selectivity of the accessible reflection operator. This bound limits the performance of NOAA in hybrid CV-DV systems. To mitigate this limitation, we propose using a squeezed CV ancilla to reduce the overlap between relevant CV states and a hybrid quantum signal processing (HQSP) filter to suppress errors arising from imperfect knowledge of the target eigenenergy. Numerical simulations show that, for small initial target-state amplitudes, our protocol achieves higher fidelity and efficiency than the repeat-until-success (RUS) method despite the presence of non-orthogonality. For large initial amplitudes, RUS is already efficient, and amplitude amplification provides little additional advantage.
item.dc:creator: Jiyuan Liu, Joel Bierman, Yuan Liu

item.title: What Does the Effective Dimension of a Hybrid Quantum Neural Network Actually Measure?
item.description: arXiv:2610.14070v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hybrid quantum neural networks (QNNs) pass features from a classical backbone into a variational quantum circuit, and many studies log a scalar called the effective dimension as a sign of capacity or model quality. The effective dimension is usually defined as the participation ratio (PR) of the quantum Fisher information matrix (QFIM), but studies in practice log a PR of cheap parameter sensitivities instead, and the meaning of that scalar is rarely tested. We show that the logged scalar equals the PR of Pauli-Z output sensitivities, that each sensitivity is at most n times its QFIM diagonal entry on n qubits, and that a PR of the QFIM diagonal overstates the full-matrix PR by an exact factor set by the off-diagonal mass. We then test the scalar on CIFAR-10 and EuroSAT with four frozen backbones, one of them a random projection, over 4 to 16 qubits, 1 to 4 layers, three entangling patterns, and three seeds. At a fixed circuit, CIFAR-10 accuracy spans 23.14% to 86.44% while the scalar stays between 6.63 and 9.13, and its correlation with accuracy changes sign across seeds in 7 of the 14 configurations. Depth raises the share of active parameters from 0.39 to 0.91, near a ceiling we derive, and initial gradient variance falls by a factor of 34.5 from 4 to 16 qubits. Removing entanglement raises accuracy by 5.3 to 8.2 points at the same parameter count. The effective dimension therefore describes circuit geometry rather than model quality, so capacity, trainability, and accuracy each need their own diagnostic.
item.dc:creator: Md Masum Mia, Amith Khandakar, Mohamed Arselene Ayari

item.title: Resolving Nonlocal State Reduction via Induced Coherence in Frequency-Comb Biphoton Sources
item.description: arXiv:2610.27602v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: How macroscopic definite outcomes and nonlocal correlations emerge from entangled superpositions across spacelike-separated regions without superluminal action or {\it ad hoc} wavefunction collapse remains a defining open question in the foundations of quantum mechanics. Here, we resolve this century-long paradox within \textit{linear} relativistic quantum electrodynamics by developing an open-system and measurement-defined framework realized in dual, spacelike-separated nonlinear crystals driven synchronously by a multi-mode optical frequency comb and seeded by an ultra-narrow coherent laser. Expanding the transverse electromagnetic vector potential into discrete single-photon frequency-comb supermodes, we show that tracing out the unmeasured continuous-wave idler field yields an exact spatial dephasing Lindblad master equation whose decoherence rate is governed by the non-orthogonal state overlap of single-photon-added coherent states. Connecting this open-system map to free-vector-space quotient measurement theory, we demonstrate that single-particle interference arises from the geometric projection of the composite state onto detector-defined conditional cosets rather than remote collapse, establishing strict operational equivalence across pump, seed, and signal phase scans. The resulting wave-particle-entanglement triality equality $P^2 + E^2 + V^2 = 1$ is saturated across the complete parameter space, while the atomic-clock-referenced comb structure anchors continuous-variable time-frequency displacement stabilizers directly at the hardware layer. Our work unifies induced coherence, Bohr's complementarity, and quotient measurement theory, providing a microscopic pathway toward fault-tolerant bosonic quantum information processing.
item.dc:creator: Tai Hyun Yoon

item.title: Post-Quantum Perfect Zero-Knowledge Arguments for NP From Any One-Way Permutation
item.description: arXiv:2610.33185v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we show for the first time that post-quantum one-way permutations are sufficient for perfect zero-knowledge classical arguments for all of NP with security guaranteed against quantum adversaries. We first establish that Naor, Ostrovsky, Venkatesan, and Yung's bit commitment scheme built from any permutation using interactive hashing, called the NOVY scheme, is sum-binding and collapse-binding against quantum polynomial-time committers provided the permutation is post-quantum one-way. We then show that the collapse-binding property of the NOVY scheme allows for Blum's perfect zero-knowledge argument for HAMCYCLE to remain so exactly as it stands against quantum adversaries.
item.dc:creator: Fr\'ed\'eric Dupuis, R\'emi Ligez, Khaireddine Medhioub, Louis Salvail, Louis-Charles Thibodeau

item.title: Population Capacity and the Geometry of Thermomajorization
item.description: arXiv:2610.35433v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We characterize finite-dimensional quasiclassical state conversion under thermal operations through population capacities: the maximum population that thermal operations can concentrate on each subset of energy levels. We show that these capacities form a normalized, nondecreasing submodular rank function whose base polytope coincides with the thermally reachable population region. This representation provides complete accessibility constraints and a greedy construction of states maximizing the expectation value of any system observable. For a prescribed target, exact conversion can be certified by the optimized responses of at most $n-1$ target-adapted binary work-extraction probes. For approximate conversion, we exploit the Lorenz-curve structure of population capacities to construct, in $O(n^2\log n)$ arithmetic and comparison operations, a reachable state that simultaneously minimizes every convex separable residual error at fixed positive comparison weights. This state also realizes a common first contact with the corresponding target-centered smoothing regions. Finally, the optimal trace-distance error equals the largest capacity advantage of the target over the initial state, attained at a target thermomajorization prefix and determined by the same optimized binary-probe responses. Thus population capacities provide a unified, constructive framework for thermal accessibility, observable optimization, conversion certification, and universal approximation.
item.dc:creator: F. Meroi, C. Massri, M. Losada, G. Bellomo, G. M. Bosyk

item.title: Quantum communication: a discrimination approach
item.description: arXiv:2610.40358v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a state discrimination approach to unassisted quantum communication through a noisy quantum channel. Starting from the operational duality between entanglement recovery and state discrimination, we construct entanglement-generation codes with explicit decoders constructed from Petz recovery maps. The resulting error bounds hold for every number of channel uses and are expressed in terms of Petz-R\'enyi coherent information. For product sources, they yield exponential error decay at rates below coherent information.
item.dc:creator: Hao-Chung Cheng

item.title: Seeing Why: Exact Evidence Maps for Quantum and Optical Image Classifiers
item.description: arXiv:2611.01993v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When an image classifier decides, we can usually only estimate why. For quantum and all-optical classifiers that act linearly on amplitude-encoded pictures up to the measurement, with no trained classical network before or after them, each class's Born probability above its no-information share, $P_g - b_g$, splits exactly into contributions of the encoded amplitudes, shown as Born evidence maps (BEM). The split itself follows from known results on quadratic forms: with the transmitted light held fixed, it is what Integrated Gradients from a zero baseline and the Shapley value give. What we add is a way to measure it on the hardware that classifies, from class probabilities on a quantum chip or, in simulation, from camera frames on a lens bench, with no gradient circuit and no light sent backwards; a $g\times g$ map takes $1 + 2g^2$ runs. Deleting the 5% of pixels with the highest evidence drops accuracy from 73% to 9% (one seed), as occlusion and gradient $\times$ input do, while plain gradients remove much less. The classifiers share one architecture, a Fourier-plane mask followed by a brickwall circuit on qubits or by phase plates on a lens bench, read by a fixed Born headroom readout with no trained parameter; centring each picture on its own mean lets dark features count as much as bright ones. In simulation, four phase plates at one wavelength reach 72.3% on Caltech-10 colour photographs. On IBM's ibm_kingston, with the mask computed classically before approximate loading, 300 test pictures were classified at 37.7% against 10% chance (56.3% in exact simulation), and $2\times2$ maps of the filtered input of 30 test pictures drawn at random in advance, measured on the chip, agreed with the exact ones ($r = 0.88$; standard estimator 0.82). The maps also revealed a shortcut in the data; as the trim that removed it was chosen on test pictures, the Caltech-10 results are exploratory.
item.dc:creator: Teerawat Tongloy, Rangsan Jomtarak

item.title: eigenkit: A Provider-Neutral Quantum Computing Library
item.description: arXiv:2611.02979v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum software ecosystems provide increasingly capable tools for simulation and hardware execution, but differences in programming models, supported features, and backend capabilities can make it difficult to move and systematically compare the same quantum algorithm across execution environments. We introduce eigenkit, a provider-neutral quantum computing library that separates algorithm definition from backend execution through a common circuit representation and provider interface. The library currently supports 12 execution providers spanning simulators and quantum hardware, provides backend-independent gradient computation, and integrates with standard scientific-computing and machine-learning workflows through NumPy, PyTorch, and scikit-learn interfaces. We evaluate the practical relevance of this abstraction across both simulation and quantum hardware. Simulator performance varies substantially with circuit size, structure, batching, and application workload, showing that no single backend is consistently preferable. On quantum hardware, experiments on IBM Heron and IQM Emerald show that which processor is better suited to a given algorithm depends not only on hardware constraints, but also on how well the topology of the quantum algorithm matches the physical connectivity of the processor. These results demonstrate that backend portability is not only a software-design convenience, but can be important for both computational efficiency and quantum execution quality.
item.dc:creator: Laia Domingo, Daniil Tarpanov, Arsenii Senokosov, Asel Sagingalieva

item.title: Symmetry-guided algorithms for variational quantum optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.05865v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum numbers associated with symmetries classify quantum states and identify the sectors relevant to a given simulation. Generic hardware-efficient ansatzes do not necessarily preserve the quantum numbers and may therefore explore states outside the target sector. We develop symmetry-guided algorithms based on the quantum-accessible Hilbert-Schmidt asymmetry $\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{HS}$, which quantifies the deviation of a quantum state from invariance under a specified symmetry group. This quantity guides the optimization toward a highly reduced symmetry-based target sector, without enforcing the symmetry on the preparation circuit. We demonstrate the approach as a proof of principle in variational quantum eigensolver calculations targeting singlet ground states with collective SU(2) symmetry. The applications include a five-qubit $S$-wave $p+{}^3\mathrm{He}$ two-cluster Hamiltonian, deduced from $\textit{ab initio}$ many-body calculations, and collective spin models with up to 12 particles, which provide a many-particle benchmark of asymmetry-guided optimization. Across these applications, $\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{HS}$-based guidance increases the singlet probability. Overall, the proposed algorithms improve energy accuracy during optimization and ground-state fidelity compared with direct energy minimization, with substantial fidelity improvements in the larger spin systems. These results demonstrate the utility of an asymmetry objective determined by the group action, independently of the Hamiltonian energy, for improving the reliability of variational quantum optimization.
item.dc:creator: Eunjin In, Kristina D. Launey, Darin C. Mumma, James A. Sauls

item.title: Helium States in a CAS(2,2) Subspace Inspired by Quantum Photonics
item.description: arXiv:2611.06448v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a four-mode Fock-state photonics implementation of the variational quantum deflation (VQD) algorithm to calculate the ground-state and excited-state energies for the neutral helium atom in a CAS(2,2) Subspace. Its CAS(2,2) electronic Hilbert space is encoded into a bosonic Fock-space representation and subsequently optimized using a continuous-variable quantum circuit. The circuit architecture under study is constructed of single-mode phase shifts, beam splitters, and cross-Kerr interactions. The variational circuit is initialized in the Fock state $\ket{1100}$ and its performance is benchmarked against exact diagonalization of the active-space configuration-interaction (CASCI) Hamiltonian. We also extend the method to optimize from the first to three excited states of the helium atom with the aid of the variational quantum deflation $(VQD)$ method in a CAS(2,2). We then investigate the performance of this circuit architecture as a basis for implementing the VQD method. In the ideal noiseless simulation setting, we see that the survival probability of the ground and the excited states within the target $CAS$ subspace is unity, because the total photon number and the photon number in the two spin sectors $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are preserved. We demonstrate that the proposed approach enables the determination of the ground and excited-state energies within the CAS(2,2) electronic Hilbert space using a continuous-variable quantum circuit and the variational quantum deflation ($VQD$) algorithm, while satisfying the orthogonality conditions with negligible errors.
item.dc:creator: Forouzan Mirmasoudi, Badie Ghavami

item.title: Cryptanalysis of Isogeny-Based Quantum Money with Rational Points
item.description: arXiv:2508.00351v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Quantum money is a representative application in cryptography that utilizes quantum technology to achieve security that is unattainable with classical systems. Since the theoretical proposal by Wiesner in 1983, the most recent instantiation is the quantum money using class group actions on elliptic curves, proposed by Montgomery and Sharif in Asiacrypt'24. In this work, we propose a concrete cryptanalysis by leveraging the efficiency of evaluating division polynomials with the coordinates of rational points, offering a speedup of $O(\log^4p)$ compared to the brute-force attack. While the resulting attack still runs in exponential time, our method provides the first nontrivial algorithmic insight into their structural hardness. Furthermore, due to the algebraic properties of rational points and quadratic twists, our technique naturally yields a more efficient verification procedure for the underlying quantum money. We believe this new line of analysis opens promising directions for future research in elliptic-curve-based quantum cryptography.
item.dc:creator: Hyeonhak Kim, Donghoe Heo, Seokhie Hong, Sangjin Lee, Suhri Kim

item.title: Optimal expansion in unitary groups I: Golden adelic groups and cutoff
item.description: arXiv:2509.09047v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this paper and its companion [DEP2] we construct and study special generating sets for $p$-arithmetic unitary Lie groups, extending the seminal works of Lubotzky, Phillips and Sarnak to higher dimensions. The real embeddings of our sets form optimal topological generators for compact unitary Lie groups, and their $p$-adic embeddings give rise to Cayley graphs and complexes over finite unitary groups, which exhibit the cutoff phenomenon. In the current paper we prove two main results: First, we construct $p$-arithmetic lattices in $PU_4$ and $PU_8$ which act transitively on their corresponding Bruhat-Tits buildings. These groups are used to construct Golden Gate sets on two and three qubits, which have optimal circuit length and efficient compiling algorithms. Second, we study the cutoff phenomenon for quotients of the Bruhat-Tits building of a general semisimple $p$-adic group. We show that cutoff occurs for quotients which satisfy either the Ramanujan property or the weaker Sarnak-Xue Density Hypothesis (SXDH). For this purpose we bound the operator norms of a large class of Hecke operators in terms of the rate of decay of unitary representations. In the companion paper [DEP2], we prove such a SXDH result for unitary groups.
item.dc:creator: Rahul Dalal, Shai Evra, Ori Parzanchevski

item.title: HomID : Benchmarking Intrinsic Dimension Estimators on Homogenous Manifolds with Anisotropic Embeddings
item.description: arXiv:2510.01335v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The manifold hypothesis suggests that data lies on manifolds with smaller intrinsic dimension (ID) than their ambient dimension. However there is no empirical agreement on the estimates for ID from different estimators for realistic datasets. Thus it is important to test ID estimators (IDEs) with targeted stressors. In this work, we consider the role of anisotropy. To this end, we propose HomID, a collection of homogeneous spaces with anisotropic embedding, for benchmarking ID estimators. We observe that methods that perform well on standard benchmarks systematically degrade on HomID under identical resource allocation. We further observe that anisotropic distortion of such benchmarks also results in performance degradation. Finally, we demonstrate that controlled anisotropic distortions induce systematic shifts in the distributions on which these methods rely, providing a concrete mechanism for the resulting estimation errors in two particular IDEs. The code for the project is available at https://github.com/a-writes-code/homid
item.dc:creator: Aritra Das, Joseph T. Iosue, Victor V. Albert

item.title: How Far Can a Trainable Frequency Move? Resolution, Grids and Coupling in Trainable-FrequencyQuantum Models
item.description: arXiv:2602.23409v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Trainable-frequency quantum models train the prefactors of their encoding gates so that the circuit's frequencies can move onto the target's. From the unit start of prior work, training rarely reaches a target more than one resolution step away. We show that the target-driven part of the prefactor gradient is a weighted sum of slopes of the overlap $\sin u/u$, where $u$ is the model-target frequency distance scaled by the window half-width. This gives each frequency a reach: under gradient flow, an isolated real frequency whose coefficient adapts optimally reaches its target from within half a step, for every target at least one step from zero frequency; with a fixed coefficient, a phase-dependent barrier can stop it. A ternary prefactor grid places a model frequency within half a step of every band frequency, with logarithmically many encoding gates. Single-frequency circuits trained with Adam and jointly trained amplitudes behave as predicted: inside the first side lobe, a frequency starts toward its target exactly when in phase with it in 98% of runs, and only 11 of 768 frequencies starting beyond the lobe reached their target. With several frequencies, the grid start raised successful fits on synthetic targets from 69% to 84% against the best random start. With many target frequencies, least squares on the fixed grid fits near-perfectly, but the circuit does not reach the coefficients; training the prefactors narrows this shortfall, but with 8 and 24 target frequencies, training the fixed grid ten times longer fitted better. On real series, training the frequencies improved held-out $R^2$ at equal budget by 0.010--0.045 on four of seven series, but a classical screen did not separate these from the others. A classical model with independently trainable frequencies shows the same dependence on the start; our results describe how to train such models, not an advantage of the circuit.
item.dc:creator: Michael Poppel, Markus Baumann, Sebastian W\"olckert, Claudia Linnhoff-Popien, Jonas Stein

item.title: Emergent thermal behavior, synchronization, and non-Hermitian phase transitions in driven-dissipative photon condensates
item.description: arXiv:2603.21927v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Driven-dissipative Bose-Einstein condensates of photons in optical resonators have been shown theoretically to exist as a long-lived, yet metastable state stabilized by a ghost attractor, despite continuous driving [Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 053402 (2025)]. Here we analyze the properties of this metastable condensate as well as the relaxation dynamics into and out of this state by means of the Lindblad master-equation approach, treating the condensate and the equal-time, noncondensed fluctuations on the same footing. Despite its nonequilibrium origin, the quasistationary condensate exhibits thermal behavior in that the order-parameter fluctuations scale with system size as in thermodynamic equilibrium, and the photon-number distribution in multimode resonators is in excellent agreement with a Bose-Einstein distribution. A linear stability analysis further reveals the presence of several exceptional points, resulting in multiple non-Hermitian phase transitions associated with the relaxation dynamics into and out of the metastable condensate. These behaviors reconcile apparently contradictory experimental results.
